clue.text: Aid to facial make-up for those who want a man

definitions.text: Aid to facial make-up for those who want a man

parts.words: Aid to facial make-up for those who want a man
parts.note: the 'facial make-up' is not cosmetics but a face assembled from stock features, and 'those who want a man' are police hunting a suspect

explanation.surface: Sounds like a cosmetics product sold to people looking for a husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make-up' reads as cosmetics and 'want a man' as romance; really it means putting a face together, for police who want (are seeking) a man.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a kit of interchangeable facial features from which police build a likeness of a wanted suspect from witness descriptions.

clue.text: Clubs best not to be clapped in

definitions.meaning: golf clubs with metal heads, as opposed to woods

definitions.text: best not to be clapped in
definitions.meaning: fetters or shackles; to be clapped in them is to be chained up as a prisoner

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clapped in irons' is the old phrase for being shackled, often aboard ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a set of metal-headed golf clubs and the chains a prisoner is put in, as in 'clapped in irons'.

clue.text: When the Levellers called it a day

definitions.text: When the Levellers called it a day

parts.words: When the Levellers called it a day
parts.note: Levellers are taken as people who make things level, so the time of day is read as the act of making even

explanation.surface: A history question about when the radical Levellers of the English Civil War gave up.
explanation.walkthrough: The Levellers were a 17th-century English political movement; here a leveller is anyone making things even, and the time of day when work stops is read as that act.
explanation.definitionFit: The late part of the day, when work is called off, is also the present participle of 'even', making level.

clue.text: Camper takes a room in Kent

definitions.note: the definition stands for a place found in Kent, a noun phrase for a town

parts.note: a camper is someone who tents, a tenter
a den is a small private room

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker in a tent rents a room somewhere in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is a county in south-east England; the answer is one of its market towns.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenterden is a market town in the Weald of Kent, so it is a place located in that county.

clue.text: Admitting to Lovers Lane?

parts.note: the thing that lets you into a lane where couples stroll is a country gate whose design is said to invite a kiss

explanation.surface: Someone confessing to having been down the local lovers' lane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admitting' looks like confessing; it means letting in, as a gate does, and 'Lovers' hints at the kiss in its name.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a small gate swinging in a U- or V-shaped enclosure, passable by one person at a time, and traditionally a place where courting couples kiss.

clue.text: Twitch a townee over

indicators.note: in a down clue 'over' tells us the word for a townee is turned backwards

parts.note: a cit is an old word for a citizen or town-dweller

explanation.surface: A town-dweller toppling over gives a nervous jerk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' reverses CIT; 'cit', short for citizen, was a scornful name for a townsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A tic is an involuntary muscular jerk, which is what a twitch is.

clue.text: A bit of a budding friend in Kent perhaps ?

parts.note: Kent is in the south-east of England, abbreviated SE
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: A gardening friend in Kent sends a cutting from something budding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link here, not a container signal: SE and PAL are side by side. 'Kent perhaps' is an example of the south-east region.
explanation.definitionFit: A sepal is one of the leaf-like parts enclosing a flower bud, so it is part of something budding.

clue.text: Returns no vote as old English joiner

indicators.note: Returns tells us the run of three short pieces is read backwards from the end

parts.note: taken as written
a vote is marked with a cross, X
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who returns a ballot marked 'no' is described as an old English carpenter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returns' turns NO + X + AS round to give SAXON. 'Joiner' suggests a carpenter, but it means one who joined with the Angles.
explanation.definitionFit: The Saxons were Germanic settlers of old England who joined with the Angles to form the Anglo-Saxons.

clue.text: There's a Dutch hooligan, on the street, officer

indicators.note: in a down clue 'on' places the first piece above the second

parts.note: the Provos were a 1960s Dutch anarchist youth movement, so a Provo is a Dutch young rebel
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A Dutch troublemaker is out on the street, and so is an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: A provost is a head of a college or, in Scotland, a mayor, and also a military police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A provost marshal is a military police officer, and provost also names other senior officials.

clue.text: Politicians who work their passage.?

parts.note: 'work their passage' suggests earning a voyage; here the passage is the lobby corridor of a parliament, where these people work on politicians

explanation.surface: Sounds like politicians paying for a sea voyage by labouring on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work one's passage' means pay one's way by working aboard ship; here the passage is the parliamentary lobby where these people do their work.
explanation.definitionFit: These are people who try to sway legislators, traditionally by buttonholing them in the lobby of the house.

clue.text: He was divine-but so wet !

parts.note: 'divine' means a god and 'wet' is a weakling, but the wetness is literal: a sea god in Greek myth

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark about a charming but feeble man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet' looks like British slang for feeble; here it is literal, as he is a god of the sea. Oceanus was the Titan who ruled the great river encircling the world.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this Titan personified the world-encircling ocean, a deity made of water.

clue.text: The conceited fool to sport a crest?

definitions.meaning: the red comb on a cockerel's head, also the jester's cap shaped like it

explanation.walkthrough: The 'to sport a' is a link: the second sense is the crest a cockerel sports.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a vain fop and, spelt as a cock's comb, the fleshy crest on a rooster's head worn also on a jester's cap.

clue.text: Baconian term of opprobrium ?

parts.note: 'Baconian' suggests the philosopher Francis Bacon, but it means to do with bacon, i.e. pigs, and the term is an insult

explanation.surface: A scholar asking what insult Francis Bacon used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baconian' points to the philosopher Francis Bacon, but bacon comes from pigs, and the word for a pig is also an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigs give bacon, and the word for a pig is also a common insult for a contemptible person.

clue.text: Itemized contents of Edison's study?

definitions.meaning: a detailed list of goods or contents
Thomas Edison was an inventor, so his study is read as a place for inventing, like a laboratory

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense treats the word as invent + -ory, like laboratory or observatory.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a detailed list of goods and, split as a place for an inventor like a laboratory, the workroom of Edison.

clue.text: Bacchus his valet

parts.note: Bacchus is the god of wine, so his emblem is the grapevine, and a valet is one who dresses his master

explanation.surface: An old-style phrase naming the servant of the wine god.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bacchus his' is the old way of writing 'Bacchus's'. A valet dresses his master, and the wine god's emblem is the grapevine, so his valet is one who dresses (prunes and trains) vines.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who prunes and tends grapevines dresses the plant that is the wine god's emblem, just as a valet dresses his master.

clue.text: No match for Big Bertha after Mons

definitions.text: No match for Big Bertha after Mons

parts.words: No match for Big Bertha after Mons
parts.note: Big Bertha was a giant German gun of the First World War; after the word Mons comes the name of another giant gun

explanation.surface: Sounds like a World War One claim that the German gun outclassed the defenders after the Battle of Mons.
explanation.walkthrough: Mons was a 1914 battle, but here it is the first half of Mons Meg, a giant medieval cannon at Edinburgh Castle; a match is an equal.
explanation.definitionFit: Mons Meg is a huge medieval bombard at Edinburgh Castle, a giant gun like Big Bertha, and the word that follows Mons in its name.

clue.text: Loud-speaker

parts.note: not an electrical loudspeaker but anything that makes a speaker's voice loud

explanation.surface: A one-word description of an electric speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen splits the word into a loud speaker: a cone that makes a voice carry.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a funnel-shaped horn for amplifying the voice, so it makes a speaker loud.

clue.text: Bad types show a ten degrees difference

indicators.note: difference suggests the letters of the phrase are made different, rearranged

explanation.surface: Thermometer readings ten degrees apart reveal some bad characters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'difference' tells us to rearrange A TEN DEGREES; 'show' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: These are people who have sunk to a low moral state, villainous or depraved sorts.

clue.text: We hear Mrs Giles's last pursuer takes wing

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the creature that takes wing, a flying mouse

indicators.note: 'We hear' signals that the description gives a sound, not a spelling

parts.note: the farmer's wife (Farmer Giles's wife) is chased by three blind mice, so the hindmost chaser is the rear mouse

explanation.surface: Someone chasing the farmer's wife suddenly flies off.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme the three blind mice all ran after the farmer's wife; Farmer Giles is the stock English farmer, so she is Mrs Giles. Reremouse is an old word for a bat, a mouse that takes wing.
explanation.definitionFit: Reremouse is an archaic word for a bat, the mouse-like creature that flies.

clue.text: Foreigner due to putt?

parts.note: on a golf course, a player about to putt has just come onto the putting surface

explanation.surface: A foreign golfer about to take a putt.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf you putt once your ball has landed on the green; read as one who lands on the green, the word names someone from the Arctic island.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a native of the Arctic island Greenland, also read as one whose ball has landed on the green.

clue.text: It muffles the drums

parts.note: the drums are not percussion but the drums of the ears

explanation.surface: Something a band uses to dampen percussion.
explanation.walkthrough: The drums are eardrums, not percussion.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a plug pushed into the ear canal to deaden sound reaching the eardrum.

clue.text: Take a pew back here-it's *the answer

indicators.note: back tells us the phrase for taking a seat is read from end to start

parts.note: 'take a pew' is a British idiom meaning sit down

explanation.surface: A churchgoer is told to sit back in a pew, as that is the answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take a pew' means sit down; 'back' reverses SIT. 'Tis is the old contraction of 'it is'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Tis is the poetic contraction of 'it is', the same as the contraction it's.

clue.text: Master Cratchit has parental refusal to be given a beating

definitions.note: a phrase for something that is beaten, here a drum

parts.note: Tiny Tim is the young son of Bob Cratchit in Dickens's A Christmas Carol
pa is a parent, father
no is a refusal

explanation.surface: Tiny Tim's father refuses him, and he is to be thrashed.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'beating' is drumming, not punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: A timpano is a single kettledrum, an instrument that is struck with sticks.

clue.text: The mayor's a vinous bird

parts.note: port is a wine, so it answers to vinous
a reeve is the female of the ruff, a wading bird

explanation.surface: The mayor is mocked as a boozy old bird.
explanation.walkthrough: A reeve is a female ruff. A portreeve was the chief officer of an English town, the forerunner of a mayor.
explanation.definitionFit: A portreeve was the chief magistrate of a medieval English town, the office later called mayor.

clue.text: How 'to, make. poor " Tom Brown?

parts.note: turning something brown is done by cooking it before a fire, and in Tom Brown's Schooldays the bully Flashman holds poor Tom before the fire

explanation.surface: A question about tanning a pale boy named Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: In Thomas Hughes's novel Tom Brown's Schooldays, set at Rugby School, Flashman holds Tom against the fire; to brown meat you cook it in that way.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooking before a fire turns meat brown, and the bully Flashman did the same to Tom in the novel.

clue.text: Is blue-and fatheaded ?

definitions.meaning: sulks, is in low spirits; to mump is to mope
having a swollen head and neck, as with the glandular illness

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fatheaded' usually means stupid; here it means literally swollen in the face.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb meaning sulks or mopes, and the viral illness that makes the face swell up.

clue.text: Boy takes two notes from a docker

indicators.note: 'takes ... from' signals that the two notes are removed from the docker

parts.note: a stevedore is one who loads and unloads ships
DO and RE are two notes of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A lad takes down two messages from a dock worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' looks like messages; it means musical notes DO and RE, which come off the end of STEVEDORE.
explanation.definitionFit: Steve is a common male first name, so it can stand for a boy.

clue.text: What a relief when the maid arrived !

definitions.text: What a relief when the maid arrived

parts.words: What a relief when the maid arrived
parts.note: the maid is Joan of Arc, and the relief is the lifting of a siege in 1429

explanation.surface: Someone thankful that the cleaner has finally turned up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maid' suggests a servant; it is Joan of Arc, the Maid who relieved the English siege of the French city in 1429.
explanation.definitionFit: Joan of Arc, called the Maid of Orléans, relieved the siege of this French city in 1429.

clue.text: Many a slip ." but if not many, one may

definitions.text: Many a slip ." but if not many, one may

indicators.note: 'if not' signals removing what follows from the word just quoted

parts.note: taken as written from the proverb
L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a crossword stand-in for many

explanation.surface: The proverb about a slip 'twixt cup and lip, with a twist.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'there's many a slip 'twixt cup and lip'; take L ('many') out of SLIP and you get what one may do between cup and lip.
explanation.definitionFit: Between cup and lip one may take a small mouthful, completing the old proverb.

clue.text: Goes out in right-minded clothing

indicators.note: 'in' tells us one word is placed inside the other

parts.note: sane means of sound mind
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sensible person goes out in proper clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes' is a link: OUT goes in SANE.
explanation.definitionFit: A soutane is a cassock, the long garment worn by Roman Catholic priests.

clue.text: Some, reel, and just one less than drunk

definitions.text: Some, reel, and just one less than drunk

parts.words: Some, reel, and just one less than drunk
parts.note: the number names a Scottish dance when 'some' is added to it, and one more than it puts you 'one over' it, which is drunk

explanation.surface: A tipsy dancer at a Scottish reel, nearly drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The eightsome reel is a Scottish country dance; 'one over the eight' is a British idiom for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: The number is the first part of the eightsome reel, and one more than it is being 'one over the eight', which means drunk.

clue.text: Letter Poe mislaid-for-Mrs :Chanticleer

definitions.note: the wife of the cockerel in Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale

indicators.note: mislaid means put in the wrong place, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A letter from Edgar Allan Poe to a woman has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mislaid' rearranges LETTER POE.
explanation.definitionFit: In Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale the cock Chanticleer's favourite hen is also his wife.
